label: Ubiquiti UniFi 5G Max Outdoor
description: Outdoor 5G NR/LTE modem: one 2.5GbE RJ45 port, PoE input, IPX6 (IP67 with cable-gland door kit).
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Networking Interface **(1) 2.5 GbE RJ45 port**, **5G NR and LTE** radio, nano-SIM or eSIM, PoE input, **IPX6 - and IP67 only with the cable-gland door kit**, 1.2 kg. The IP rating is conditional: an outdoor install without that door kit is IPX6, which is water jets from any direction but **not** dust-tight immersion protection. Price the kit in with the unit.

label: Ubiquiti UniFi Device Bridge
description: Wireless device bridge: one GbE RJ45 port, internal antenna plus an RP-SMA connector for an external omni.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Networking Interface **(1) GbE RJ45 port**, antennas **(1) internal plus (1) RP-SMA connector for an external omni-antenna**, managed over WiFi, channel bandwidth 20/40/80 MHz, 200 g. It is a **bridge, not an access point**: one copper port in, wireless across, and the external antenna connector means the range is a choice you make rather than a property of the box.

label: Ubiquiti UniFi Device Bridge IoT
description: Compact IoT wireless bridge: one 10/100M RJ45 port, internal antenna plus RP-SMA for an external omni.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Networking Interface **(1) 10/100M RJ45 port**, one internal antenna plus RP-SMA for an external omni, channel bandwidth 20/40 MHz, **45 g**. Two limits for an IoT install: the port is **fast Ethernet** so a 100 Mbps ceiling applies to everything bridged, and the radio is 20/40 MHz only - it cannot use an 80 MHz channel, which is the right trade for range but wrong if you expected the Device Bridge's rates.

label: Ubiquiti UniFi Device Bridge Pro
description: Outdoor wireless bridge: two GbE RJ45 ports, PoE input with passive PoE output, external-antenna capable.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Networking Interface **(2) GbE RJ45 ports**, management **(1) PoE in (PoE output not used) plus (1) passive PoE output**, internal antennas, wind loading 69 N at 200 km/h, 431 g. **The second port powers something else on passive PoE** - useful for a camera at the far end of a bridge, but the power comes out of the PoE input budget, and passive means the device must accept raw voltage rather than negotiate.

label: Ubiquiti UniFi EAV Bridge
description: AV-over-IP bridge: one GbE RJ45 PoE+ input port, USB-C 5V/1A port, IR 3.5 mm in/out, 1.3 inch touchscreen.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Networking Interface **(1) GbE RJ45 PoE+ In Etherlighting port**, versatile port **(1) USB Type-C 5V 1A**, IR **(1) 3.5 mm input or output**, power method PoE+, max power consumption **14 W**, 1.3 inch touchscreen. It is an **AV endpoint**, so the useful questions are PoE class (PoE+ for 14 W) and the IR/USB-C control path, not switching throughput. The USB-C port (5V 1A) and the 3.5 mm IR jack are recorded here rather than as interfaces: they are power and control paths, not data ports, and the catalogue's interface types do not cover them.

label: Ubiquiti UniFi Express 7
description: Compact Wi-Fi 7 router/AP: one 2.5GbE RJ45 and one 10GbE RJ45 port, 2.3 Gbps IDS/IPS throughput.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Port Layout **1x 2.5 GbE RJ45 (2.5G/1G/100M/10M) and 1x 10 GbE RJ45 (10G/5G/2.5G/1G/100M)**, **IDS/IPS throughput 2.3 Gbps**, coverage area 160 m2, stateful firewall and Layer 7 application-aware firewall. Two ports total: **the 10G port is the LAN side**, so this is a small-site gateway, not a distribution switch - and 2.3 Gbps of IPS is the real ceiling once inspection is on, whatever the 10G port says.

label: Ubiquiti UniFi U7 Pro
description: Ceiling Wi-Fi 7 access point with one 1/2.5GbE RJ45 port.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Networking Interface **(1) 1/2.5 GbE RJ45 port**, channel bandwidth HT 20/40, VHT 20/40/80/160 and HE up to 160 MHz, 680 g, stainless and galvanised steel mount. **The 2.5G port is the point of the model** - a Wi-Fi 7 AP on a gigabit port gives you Wi-Fi 7 radios with a gigabit bottleneck, and the 160 MHz HE channel is what makes that gap visible.

label: Ubiquiti USW Pro Max 16 PoE
description: 16-port Layer 3 switch: 12x 1G all PoE+, 4x 2.5G all PoE++, 2x 10G SFP+, 180 W PoE budget.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Port Layout **12x 1 GbE RJ45 (all PoE+), 4x 2.5 GbE RJ45 (all PoE++), 2x 10G SFP+**, **Total PoE availability 180 W**, Layer 3 supported, 1U rack/desktop/wall. **180 W across sixteen powered ports is 11 W average**: the four PoE++ ports can pass 60 W each on paper, so two 60 W devices would already take two thirds of the whole budget. The 2.5G ports are the only fast copper on the box.

label: Ubiquiti USW Pro Max 16
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Port Layout **12x 1 GbE RJ45, 4x 2.5 GbE RJ45, 2x 10G SFP+**, switching capacity 84 Gbps, non-blocking throughput 42 Gbps, Layer 3 supported. **Unlike the PoE variant of the same name there is no power on any port** - twelve 1G, four 2.5G and two SFP+, and the model number is identical apart from the suffix.

label: Ubiquiti UniFi AC Mesh
description: Outdoor 802.11ac mesh access point with one GbE RJ45 port and pole mount.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Networking Interface **(1) GbE RJ45 port**, pole mount 25-76 mm, 152 g, channel bandwidth HT 20/40 and VHT 20/40/80 MHz. **One port and one radio pair** - meshing is done over the wireless, so every hop halves the throughput available to the far side. Request #44 is the 5-pack of this model.

label: Ubiquiti UniFi AC Mesh Pro
description: Outdoor 802.11ac mesh access point with two GbE RJ45 ports and pole mount.
notes: Vendor figures from the Ubiquiti tech specs page: Networking Interface **(2) GbE RJ45 ports**, pole mount 25-63.5 mm, 633 g, channel bandwidth HT 20/40 and VHT 20/40/80 MHz. **The second port is the difference from the AC Mesh**: it lets the AP sit inline on a run and pass traffic through, which is why the Pro exists outdoors where you often have one cable and no switch.
